summary.value: The primary concerns raised by multiple reviewers are, better OOD generalization of programmatic policies is not a claim but simply an experimental observation, what constitutes minor modifications to NNs, and the experimental evaluation is limited. The authors have attempted to address the concern about OOD generalization not being a primary claim by stating it is a secondary or implicit claim. The discussion around this point revolved around semantics and was weakened by the absence of a definition of OOD generalization in the original version of this paper, and a disagreement about the appropriateness of the proposed definition. The authors did not sufficiently address the concern around what constitutes ‘minor modification’ to NN training, and some reviewers argue that changing the reward function provides another mechanism for injecting prior knowledge into training. Considering NNs are universal function approximators, the fact that a NN can be found to perform as well as the programmatic policy on generalization (or any metric) is well-understood and the paper does not expand our understanding of this phenomenon. The limited experimental evaluation is justified by the authors as necessary since these are the environments used in previous work. However, reviewers assert that additional environments would strengthen the paper’s claims.

reviewer_concerns.value: The primary contribution of the paper is an attempt to challenge the claim of superior OOD generalization of programmatic policies when compared to NNs. The reviewers concerns are two-fold, (i) existing work has not made this claim, only observed generalization in some experiments, and (ii) the fact that modifying the NN or its training is likely to provide better OOD generalization is know and not contested by existing work. The authors have not provided conclusive evidence against these criticisms.

reviewer_scores.value: I do not think the reviewers would have changed their score even if the discussion had continued unimpeded.
